story.title: FIFA Announces Co-hosts for 2031 Women's World Cup
story.summary: FIFA has confirmed that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be co-hosted by the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica. This tournament will be notable as it will feature 48 teams for the first time. Additionally, the United Kingdom has been selected to host the 2035 Women's World Cup.

explore_lenses.label: How will the 48-team tournament work?
explore_lenses.title: A longer World Cup with 104 matches
explore_lenses.summary: FIFA has set the basic competitive structure for 2031, making it substantially larger than the 32-team tournament in 2027. The qualification allocation and detailed competition regulations have not yet been announced.

claims.text: FIFA decided in May 2025 that the Women’s World Cup would expand from 32 to 48 teams beginning in 2031, following consultation with confederations and other stakeholders.
The format is planned as 12 groups, with 104 matches rather than 64 and a tournament extended by one week.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the expansion is intended to broaden elite-competition access and help more member associations develop women’s-football structures.

points: FIFA decided in May 2025 that the Women’s World Cup would expand from 32 to 48 teams beginning in 2031, following consultation with confederations and other stakeholders.
The format is planned as 12 groups, with 104 matches rather than 64 and a tournament extended by one week.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the expansion is intended to broaden elite-competition access and help more member associations develop women’s-football structures.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: FIFA has not yet published the 2031 qualifying-slot distribution, qualification calendar, draw procedures, or full tournament regulations.

explore_lenses.label: Which cities and stadiums will host matches?
explore_lenses.title: The four hosts are confirmed, venues are not
explore_lenses.summary: The host countries are appointed, but the final match footprint remains a planning decision. The bid’s venue list is a proposal rather than a confirmed schedule.

claims.text: U.S. Soccer says host cities, stadiums, match schedules, ticketing and tournament operations will be announced later with FIFA and the four host federations.
The bid included 20 potential stadiums: 14 in the United States, four in Mexico, and one each in Costa Rica and Jamaica.

FIFA’s pre-award evaluation found the joint submission met the minimum hosting requirements after an assessment that included inspection visits and criteria such as infrastructure, services, commercial matters, sustainability and human rights.

explore_lenses.label: What legacy are the hosts promising?
explore_lenses.title: A regional growth and reinvestment pledge
explore_lenses.summary: The organizing federations frame the tournament as a way to grow girls’ and women’s football across Concacaf, rather than only as a U.S.-led event. Those legacy outcomes are commitments and ambitions, not guaranteed results.

claims.text: The four federations said they would work with FIFA and Concacaf on girls’ player development, coaching education and infrastructure investment across FIFA member associations.
The original bid pledged to reinvest proceeds into global development of the women’s game and projected 4.5 million attendees; these were bid commitments and estimates, not FIFA-guaranteed outcomes.
Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will host the senior Women’s World Cup for the first time; the United States previously hosted in 1999 and 2003.

U.S. Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone said the organizers’ ambition is to make the women’s game the world’s most commercially successful sport and reinvest resulting funds into the girls’ and women’s game.

story_report.summary: FIFA has awarded the 2031 Women’s World Cup to a four-country hosting group of the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while selecting the United Kingdom for the 2035 edition. The 2031 competition will be the first Women’s World Cup with 48 teams, expanding the event beyond its previous 32-team format. Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will stage the senior tournament for the first time; the United States previously hosted in 1999 and 2003.

sections.heading: Expanded 2031 tournament format
sections.body: FIFA decided in May 2025 to expand the Women’s World Cup to 48 teams beginning in 2031 following consultation with confederations and other stakeholders. The planned format calls for 12 groups, 104 matches instead of 64, and a tournament extended by one week. FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the change is intended to widen access to elite competition and support the development of women’s-football structures among more member associations.

sections.heading: Host planning and venue selection
sections.body: The joint bid identified 20 potential stadiums: 14 in the United States, four in Mexico, and one each in Costa Rica and Jamaica. FIFA’s pre-award assessment found the proposal met minimum hosting requirements after inspection visits and reviews of infrastructure, services, commercial issues, sustainability and human rights. U.S. Soccer says host cities, stadiums, schedules, ticketing and operational arrangements will be announced later with FIFA and the four host federations.

sections.heading: Development pledges and attendance projections
sections.body: The four federations said they plan to work with FIFA and Concacaf on girls’ player development, coaching education and infrastructure investment across FIFA member associations. Their original bid also pledged to reinvest proceeds in the global women’s game and projected 4.5 million attendees. Those commitments and attendance figures are bid estimates rather than FIFA-guaranteed outcomes; U.S. Soccer President Cindy Parlow Cone said organizers aim to build commercial success and reinvest funds in girls’ and women’s football.

unresolved.text: FIFA has not published the 2031 qualifying-slot allocation, qualification calendar, draw procedures or full tournament regulations.
The final distribution of matches among the four hosts, including the venues for the opening match and final, has not been confirmed.
No binding post-tournament benchmarks have been published for investment, participation growth, facilities or the distribution of proceeds.

related_stories.title: India Commits $1.6 Billion in Flood Relief to Nepal During Prime Minister's Visit
related_stories.summary: India has pledged $1.6 billion in flood relief to Nepal as Prime Minister Balendra Shah visits New Delhi. This marks Shah's first international trip since taking office in March. The visit also resulted in agreements on infrastructure projects, including a railway and a hydropower plant.

related_stories.title: Trump Claims Role in Jensen Huang's Return to Nvidia Amid National Security Concerns
related_stories.summary: President Trump has claimed credit for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, stating he communicated with the company's board to address concerns regarding national security. He emphasized that the government does not view Huang's return as a risk to national security and described the announcement as vital for Nvidia's success and the economy.

related_stories.title: U.S. Places Megaspeed on Trade Blacklist Amid Nvidia Scandal
related_stories.summary: The U.S. government has added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, citing the firm's alleged connections to espionage and its role in the Nvidia scandal. This decision follows scrutiny over the company's ties to China and its controlling shareholder, Alice Huang, who has been implicated in an espionage investigation. The announcement coincided with the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

related_stories.title: South Korea's Education Minister Resigns Amid AI Cheating Controversy
related_stories.summary: Choi Kyo-jin, South Korea's education minister, has stepped down following backlash over last-minute security measures aimed at preventing AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam. The measures, which included the use of hidden cameras and smart glasses, sparked significant criticism and chaos during the exam process.
